meta.note: RENAMED: Cloud Functions is now Cloud Run functions, and its documentation has moved under Cloud Run. The generations are relabelled Cloud Run functions (1st gen) and (2nd gen) rather than gen1/gen2. The write-up already described gen2 as running on Cloud Run, so the substance was right and only the naming had moved. Slug kept as cloud-functions.

name: Cloud Run functions
oneLiner: Event-driven serverless functions for glue and lightweight processing.
whatItIs: Cloud Functions is Google Cloud's serverless functions service: you deploy a single function and it runs in response to events — a file arriving in Cloud Storage, a Pub/Sub message, an HTTP request — scaling automatically and billing only while it runs. No servers to manage. The 2nd generation is built on Cloud Run and Eventarc, giving longer timeouts, more memory and a broader set of event sources. In data pipelines it's the lightweight glue: react to events, do small transforms, and trigger heavier services like Dataflow or BigQuery. It's not for long-running heavy compute — it's for short, event-driven tasks.

inPractice.narrative: A file lands in a Cloud Storage bucket. That event triggers a Cloud Function that validates the file, writes metadata to Firestore, and publishes a Pub/Sub message that kicks off a Dataflow job for the real processing. Another function runs on a Pub/Sub message to call an API and load a small result into BigQuery. Each runs only when its event fires and costs nothing idle. Cloud Functions is the event-driven wiring, not the heavy lifter.
flow: trigger Dataflow / write Firestore / load BigQuery

coreConcepts.detail: Functions fire on Cloud Storage events, Pub/Sub messages, Firestore changes, HTTP requests and (via Eventarc in gen2) many more sources — you write logic, not pollers.
Gen2 is built on Cloud Run + Eventarc, offering longer timeouts (up to 60 min for HTTP), more memory/CPU, concurrency per instance, and broader events than gen1.
Billed by invocations and compute time (vCPU/memory × duration), plus networking; idle functions cost nothing — serverless economics.
Each invocation is stateless in a temporary environment; persist state to Cloud Storage/Firestore/BigQuery. Instances are reused warm when possible.
New/scaled-out instances initialise with some latency; setting minimum instances keeps a few warm for latency-sensitive functions.
Gen2 can handle multiple concurrent requests per instance (Cloud Run model), improving efficiency versus gen1's one-request-per-instance.

whenToUse: Lightweight transforms, validation and small API calls.
Triggering heavier jobs (Dataflow, BigQuery loads) from events.
HTTP endpoints/webhooks without managing a server.
Spiky workloads that should scale to zero when idle.
whenNotToUse: Long-running or heavy compute — use Dataflow/Dataproc or Cloud Run jobs.
Sustained high-throughput services where a running container is cheaper.
Large stateful in-memory processing — functions are stateless/ephemeral.
Complex multi-service apps better served directly by Cloud Run.

keyFacts.label: Billing
keyFacts.value: Per invocation + compute time (vCPU/mem × duration) + networking.

pricingShape: Cloud Functions bills for invocations plus compute time (vCPU and memory times duration) and networking, with a free tier — idle means (near) zero cost, busy scales with work. Levers mirror other FaaS: right-size memory/CPU (more can mean shorter, cheaper runs), keep functions fast, and use minimum instances only when cold starts genuinely hurt (that adds a standing cost). For steady high-volume traffic, a continuously-running Cloud Run service can be cheaper than per-invocation functions — switch when throughput is sustained.
gotchas: Gen1 vs gen2 differ significantly (timeouts, events, concurrency) — use gen2 for new work and check feature parity.
Cold starts add latency on scale-out; set minimum instances for latency-sensitive paths (at a cost).
Functions are stateless — persist anything durable to GCS/Firestore/BigQuery, not local disk.
A function writing to the bucket/topic that triggers it can create infinite loops and runaway cost.
Heavy or long jobs don't belong here — trigger Dataflow/Dataproc instead of forcing big work into a function.
